Protesters denounce Indonesian ‘waste’. G7 vote to increase sanctions on Russia. Burnham moves to oust Starmer.

Iran: The United States and Iran signed a ceasefire deal on Thursday Australian time that included reopening the Strait of Hormuz, but tensions remain over Iran’s nuclear program and Israel’s campaign against Hezbollah.

Despite US President Donald Trump insisting on Tuesday the war would soon be in the “rear-view mirror”, the initial deal – which Vice President J. D. Vance admitted was “very general” – left significant sources of tension unresolved. The deal removed restrictions on shipping in the strait but was vague about whether Tehran can eventually impose fees. Iranian mines in the strait may also discourage ships from transiting, though it was not clear whether the US Navy would be allowed to continue its mine-clearing operations.

The deal called for at least 60 days of negotiations but said Iran will not develop nuclear weapons and will dilute its stockpile of highly enriched uranium. Trump and Iran’s president, Masoud Pezeshkian, signed the deal ahead of a formal signing ceremony on Friday.

The deal also included an end to the fighting between Israel and Hezbollah, an Iran-backed group in Lebanon, but US officials said it did not require that Israel withdraw from territory it holds in southern Lebanon.

Abbas Araghchi, Iran’s foreign affairs minister, told a group of diplomats on Tuesday Iran expected Israel to withdraw from Lebanon as part of the deal. “Without the withdrawal of Israeli forces from the territories they occupied in this war, the war has not fully ended,” he said.

The deal has also led to tensions between Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who together launched the war against Iran on February 28.

Trump this week criticised Netanyahu’s handling of the campaign against Hezbollah, saying he expected Netanyahu to be “more responsible” in Lebanon.

“Israel has been fighting Hezbollah for too long and too many people are being killed,” Trump said.

Netanyahu, who faces an election later this year, has been criticised in Israel over the US–Iran deal, which failed to end Iran’s nuclear program but paved the way for sanctions to be lifted. The deal also reportedly included plans for a US$300 billion fund that will involve private businesses from the Gulf and elsewhere investing in Iran. The fund – and the end of sanctions – will depend on the outcome of talks between Tehran and Washington.

Netanyahu this week acknowledged the deal had caused tensions with Trump, telling reporters: “There are cases in which President Trump and I do not see eye to eye.”

Indonesia: Protesters in Indonesia have attacked the government over the rising cost of living and demanded an end to “wasteful” spending, which they claim included a controversial scheme to provide free meals to children and pregnant women.

A series of student-led protests across the country this week and last week warned that the country is headed for bankruptcy and called for an easing of fuel and food prices to assist struggling households. The government recently increased fuel prices by 32 per cent.

Recent increases in fuel and food prices have come as the Bank of Indonesia lifted interest rates in a move aimed at boosting confidence in the weak currency.

The protesters presented six demands to the government, including ending President Subianto Prabowo’s flagship meals scheme as well as another big-spending program to support rural villages. The meals scheme aims to address malnutrition but costs about US$15 billion a year and has resulted in mass poisonings and corruption allegations.

“People will not be silent, they will speak out when they cannot eat, cannot work, cannot have a decent life,” Jordan, a student, told Associated Press at a demonstration last week.

Ukraine: The leaders of the Group of Seven advanced economies agreed this week to increase sanctions on Russian oil and gas exports, as heavy Russian shelling on Monday and Tuesday killed at least 19 people across Ukraine.

At a meeting at the French resort town of Évian-les-Bains, European members of the G7 urged the forum to renew its focus on addressing the war in Ukraine after its recent preoccupation with the conflict in the Middle East.

Donald Trump indicated he was willing to resume sanctions on Russian oil exports after scaling back sanctions to boost energy supplies following the closure of the Strait of Hormuz.

“Soon we’ll be able to do that because the oil is now flowing,” he told reporters.

Trump met with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky during the summit and later called for Russia to make a deal to end the war.

“The whole thing is ridiculous,” he said. “So, yeah, I’m going to do whatever I can.”

Ukraine has started to make advances on the battlefield in recent weeks but has struggled to defend against large-scale Russian missile and drone attacks on Ukrainian cities.

Zelensky urged the G7 leaders to boost military support for Ukraine, including providing more air defence missiles.

Russian missile and drone strikes this week hit cities across Ukraine, while a Ukrainian drone attack in the Russian city of Tula killed three people.

On Monday, the Russian attacks hit the roof of Dormition Cathedral in the Kyiv-Pechersk Lavra, a monastery complex that was founded in 1051 and houses some of the country’s most precious religious relics and texts.

The head of the Orthodox Church of Ukraine, Metropolitan Epiphanius, said on social media the attack was a “Russian crime against humanity, against history, against Christianity”.

United Kingdom: In 2016, Andy Burnham, a former cabinet minister who had twice contested and lost the Labour Party leadership, made the unusual decision to run for mayor of the Greater Manchester region.

He insisted he did not see the role as a “stepping stone” to becoming prime minister. Instead, he said, he wanted to demonstrate that Labour could address the needs of northern cities such as Manchester, saying Westminster had an “in-built London bias”.

But, after nine years as mayor, Burnham, who is 56 years old, decided to return to parliament. On Thursday, he contested a byelection in Makerfield in northern England as part of a plan to oust Keir Starmer as Labour leader and prime minister.

Starmer has refused to resign despite a series of scandals and missteps and concerns about Labour’s prospects following its recent dismal results in local elections. The party won just 1068 council seats, down from 2566, compared with 1454 seats for Nigel Farage’s far-right Reform UK party. A YouGov poll on Tuesday found 24 per cent of people support Reform UK, compared with 19 per cent each for Labour and the Conservatives, 15 per cent for the Greens, 13 per cent for the Liberal Democrats and 9 per cent for others.

Starmer has not faced a partyroom challenge, mainly because Labour has no strong contender. But Burnham’s move back to parliament would present Labour with a serious alternative. Described as a “mild-mannered populist”, Burnham’s supporters believe he could win back support from working-class voters who have shifted to Reform UK. Polls suggest a switch from Starmer to Burnham would improve Labour’s position, though not dramatically.

A Makerfield voter, Mike Irving, told Sky News this week he had never voted Labour but was likely to back Burnham because “he’s from around here … it could impact Makerfield now”.

“We’ve got a voice here to change the country,” he said.
